batchName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

questions.question: Which Roman historian wrote the fullest account of the early Republic's debt crisis?
questions.explanation: Livy wrote the fullest account of these years. He tells the story of a ruined former soldier that captured the angry mood of 495 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Livy, the Roman historian who wrote the fullest account of these years nearly five centuries later, tells a story that captures the mood.

questions.question: What is the core problem for historians studying the early Conflict of the Orders?
options: The surviving laws cannot be read
No one wrote about the events at the time
All the records were burned by invaders
The only sources are written in Greek
questions.explanation: No one recorded these events at the time. The fullest accounts come from Livy and others writing more than four centuries later.
questions.sourceQuote: The core problem is that no one wrote about these events at the time.

questions.question: Whom did the Senate send to negotiate with the plebeians on the Sacred Mount?
questions.explanation: The Senate chose Menenius Agrippa, a former consul trusted by ordinary Romans. Tradition says he won the strikers over with a story rather than threats.
questions.sourceQuote: It chose Menenius Agrippa, a former consul who was well liked by ordinary Romans.

questions.question: According to tradition, who killed Verginia to save her from Appius Claudius?
questions.explanation: Her father killed her to uphold her freedom and virtue. He was a respected centurion, and the killing set off riots.
questions.sourceQuote: To save her from Appius Claudius, her father killed her himself, to uphold her freedom and virtue.

questions.question: In Menenius Agrippa's traditional fable, which part of the body did the limbs grow angry with?
questions.explanation: The limbs resented the belly for enjoying food while they did all the work. When they starved it, they wasted away too.
questions.sourceQuote: Once, he said, the limbs of the body grew angry with the belly.

questions.question: According to Livy, what were the Twelve Tables engraved on?
questions.explanation: Livy says the Tables were engraved on bronze and displayed publicly. That way every citizen could know the law.
questions.sourceQuote: According to Livy they were engraved on bronze and displayed publicly so every citizen could know them.

questions.question: What did one modern scholar argue about the Conflict of the Orders?
options: That there was no conflict at all
That it began under the kings
That it lasted only a single year
questions.explanation: One scholar argued there was no conflict at all. On this view, later Romans projected their own class struggles onto a dimly remembered past.
questions.sourceQuote: One modern scholar has even argued there was no conflict at all, and that later Romans projected the class struggles of their own day onto a dimly remembered past.

questions.question: What was the first office in Rome open to commoners?
questions.explanation: The tribune of the plebs was the great prize won by the first secession. Tradition says the first tribunes took office in 493 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: The great prize of the first secession of 494 BC was the tribune of the plebs, the first office in Rome open to commoners.

questions.question: What was the moral of Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly?
options: Rome's people must always obey the consuls
Rome must conquer new land to feed its people
The poor should work harder if they want to eat
Rome needs patricians and plebeians to work together
questions.explanation: Like a body, Rome could only survive if its parts cooperated. The plebeians agreed to negotiate, but wanted more than a fable.
questions.sourceQuote: Rome, like a body, could not survive unless patricians and plebeians worked together.

questions.question: Where did the plebeians camp during the first secession of 494 BC?
questions.explanation: They camped on the Mons Sacer, the 'Sacred Mount', a hill just over three miles from the city. There they built simple defences and waited.
questions.sourceQuote: Advised by Sicinius, the plebeian leader who masterminded the walkout, they left the city together and camped on the Mons Sacer, the "Sacred Mount", a hill just over three miles away.
